clue.text: A DIY magazine?

parts.note: 'DIY' (do it yourself) suggests a home-improvement periodical, but here it describes a shop where customers fetch goods themselves, and a magazine is a storehouse

explanation.surface: A periodical for home-improvement hobbyists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Magazine' tempts you towards a publication; read it as a store, and 'DIY' as shoppers serving themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop where customers pick goods off the shelves themselves is one they 'do themselves', and magazine is an old word for a storehouse.

clue.text: Parson crazed with love for a trebly gifted female

indicators.note: crazed means driven mad, so the letters of the words beside it are thrown into a new order

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, the letter O

explanation.surface: A clergyman maddened by passion for a talented woman singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazed' scrambles PARSON with O (love) to give the singer.
explanation.definitionFit: A soprano sings the highest voice part, the treble range, so she is a female gifted in the treble.

clue.text: A silly fellow set up for sponging, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the whole phrase is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a silly fellow is a fool

explanation.surface: A foolish man has been framed, ripe to be taken advantage of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' turns A FOOL upwards, giving LOOFA; 'sponging' looks like scrounging but means washing with a sponge.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofa is the dried fibrous gourd used as a bath sponge.

clue.text: Fellowships with shared interests

parts.note: a plain description of clubs or associations of people who come together over a common pursuit

explanation.definitionFit: Clubs and associations are groups of members bound by a common pursuit.

clue.text: A bird to inveigh against humanity

definitions.meaning: a marsh bird of the crake family

explanation.surface: A bird that scolds mankind.
explanation.definitionFit: The water bird is a small wader, and to protest bitterly against something is also this word, as in railing at fate.

clue.text: Its destiny may well be to chill the spirit

definitions.text: Its destiny may well be to chill the spirit

parts.words: Its destiny may well be to chill the spirit
parts.note: 'may well' hides water drawn from a well, and 'chill the spirit' means cooling a glass of whisky, not frightening the soul

explanation.surface: Something fated to dampen one's mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may well be' reads as 'quite possibly', but hints at water from a well; 'spirit' is the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Chilled drinking water is added to a glass of whisky or gin to cool it.

clue.text: Relieved of a seed, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals that these letters could form another word if rearranged

explanation.surface: Freed from a pip or seed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges A SEED.
explanation.definitionFit: Pain that has eased has been lessened or alleviated.

clue.text: No mean poet?

parts.note: 'no mean' usually means very good, but here describes someone not stingy, who also shares a name with the twentieth-century English poet Stephen

explanation.surface: A praise of a skilled writer of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Spender was an English poet; someone who is not mean with money spends freely.
explanation.definitionFit: A free-handed person splashes out money, and Stephen of that surname wrote poetry.

clue.text: Entrancing feature, possibly cleaned by…

parts.note: 'entrancing' reads as enchanting, but means belonging to an entrance; the ellipsis runs on into the next clue's cleaner

explanation.surface: A captivating attraction that someone scrubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrancing' is split as entrance-ing: the step at a front door, traditionally scrubbed by the household's daily help.
explanation.definitionFit: The step outside a house's front entrance is the classic thing a cleaning lady scrubs.

clue.text: Denounce what plagiarists do in plain language

indicators.note: in places what plagiarists do inside the plain language

parts.note: prose is ordinary language, not verse
plagiarists crib, copying others' work

explanation.surface: Condemn copying in no-nonsense terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what plagiarists do' is a verb phrase standing for the single verb crib; 'plain language' means ordinary prose rather than verse.
explanation.definitionFit: To proscribe is to condemn or outlaw something formally.

clue.text: See 1
A wrongly named fillet

indicators.note: wrongly suggests the letters are put down in the wrong order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cut of meat with the incorrect label.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrongly' rearranges A NAMED. A fillet here is a headband, not a cut of meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A fillet is a band or garland worn round the head, which is what this old poetic word means.

clue.text: Didn't take the proper course, apparently

definitions.text: Didn't take the proper course, apparently

parts.words: Didn't take the proper course, apparently
parts.note: describes someone who strayed off the route, reading 'course' as a path rather than a set of lessons

explanation.surface: Someone who seems to have skipped the right training.
explanation.definitionFit: Straying from the set path is to roam aimlessly off it.

clue.text: Pushkin hero a singular spirit?

parts.note: singular means one in number
gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: Was the Russian poet's protagonist a unique soul?
explanation.walkthrough: Eugene Onegin is the hero of Pushkin's verse novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene of that surname is the title character of Pushkin's verse novel.

clue.text: … a common daily

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a commonplace cleaning lady.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 8 Down; 'daily' there suggests a cleaner, but here means happening each day.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinary things are routine, and things done each day are routine too.

clue.text: One who is willing to take part in a Devon hill-trial?

parts.note: a trial is a test
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor in Devon

explanation.surface: A volunteer for a hill race in Devon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'willing' means making a will. Tors are rocky hilltops on Dartmoor in Devon, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who makes a will leaving property is a testator.

clue.text: Permission to view?

parts.note: reads like leave to inspect a house, but describes the British permit paid for in order to watch broadcasts

explanation.surface: A request to look round a property.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a household must buy an annual permit to watch television.
explanation.definitionFit: The annual British fee grants the legal right to watch broadcast programmes.

clue.text: A light horse man I cunningly associate with polo

indicators.note: cunningly suggests the letters are craftily rearranged

explanation.surface: A rider and I cleverly tie a pale steed to a polo game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cunningly' rearranges MAN I and POLO.
explanation.definitionFit: A golden-coated horse with a pale mane and tail is pale in colour, so light.

clue.text: Cruelly hammers a place in Bucks

indicators.note: cruelly suggests a battering that knocks the letters out of order

explanation.surface: Someone harshly pounding a town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cruelly' rearranges HAMMERS A. Bucks is Buckinghamshire, a county north-west of London; Amersham is a town there.
explanation.definitionFit: A market town in Buckinghamshire, England.

clue.text: A female science graduate posing a drainage problem for the doctor!

definitions.text: a drainage problem for the doctor

parts.note: a BSc is a Bachelor of Science
-ess is a suffix marking a female, as in lioness

explanation.surface: A woman with a science degree causes the physician difficulties.
explanation.definitionFit: A pocket of pus must be lanced and drained by a medic.

clue.text: A blunder made by backward scholars

indicators.note: backward means the word is read from its end to its start

parts.note: pupils are scholars at school

explanation.surface: An error committed by slow students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' turns PUPILS around; it looks like a description of the scholars.
explanation.definitionFit: A mistake or error.

clue.text: Sanctimonious rascal dug out in South America?

parts.note: pi is short for pious, sanctimonious
a rogue is a rascal

explanation.surface: A self-righteous villain unearthed in South America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dug out' is a dugout canoe, not excavated.
explanation.definitionFit: A canoe hollowed out of a tree trunk, used in Central and South America.

clue.text: A chaplain in the jet set, maybe?

definitions.meaning: a slang term for a clergyman, especially a forces padre
a pilot of a jet in the sky

explanation.surface: A clergyman who mixes with glamorous travellers.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a padre or clergyman, literally one who steers heavenwards; equally an airman flying jets.

clue.text: To write up when it comes out is fatuous

indicators.note: it comes out means the word it sits on the outside of the other piece
in a down clue, up means the word is read upwards

parts.note: to pen is to write

explanation.surface: Writing something down on publication is foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when it comes out' says the clue word 'it' sits on the outside; 'up' turns the verb for write, which reads upwards in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolish and clumsy, lacking sense.

clue.text: The man in charge of the cricketing board

definitions.text: The man in charge of the cricketing board

parts.words: The man in charge of the cricketing board
parts.note: suggests a cricket administrator, but the board is the scoreboard, kept by the official who records runs

explanation.surface: The head of a cricket governing body.
explanation.definitionFit: The official who records runs and wickets keeps the score on the board.

clue.text: Commonwealth pachyderm?

parts.note: split as 'common wealth', ordinary money; old British slang for money shares a name with a thick-skinned horned beast

explanation.surface: A large animal from a Commonwealth country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonwealth' splits into common wealth, and the old British slang word for money is also the name of the horned animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Dated British slang for cash is the same as the name of the horned African animal.

clue.text: Pointed attempt to draw blood

definitions.meaning: a try or go at something

explanation.surface: A sharp effort to wound.
explanation.definitionFit: A try is a go at something, and to knife someone is to wound them.

clue.text: A seer ordered to get off the mark

indicators.note: ordered means the letters are arranged in a different order

explanation.surface: A prophet was told to start scoring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' rearranges A SEER. 'get off the mark' sounds like starting to score, but means remove a mark.
explanation.definitionFit: To rub out a mark is to remove it.

clue.text: Meaning to explain how nurses spend their time?

definitions.meaning: planning or purposing to do something
nurses spend their time tending patients, read as two words

explanation.surface: An attempt to describe nurses' working day.
explanation.definitionFit: Planning to do something; split in two, it describes nurses occupied in looking after patients.

clue.text: Vexatious book in which Russian money is invested

indicators.note: invested means placed inside, as money is put into something

parts.note: a tome is a large book
the rouble is Russia's currency

explanation.surface: An annoying volume into which Russian cash has been put.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invested' plays on putting money into something: the Russian currency is placed inside the big book.
explanation.definitionFit: Annoying and causing difficulty.
